messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun was twenty years old and a writer, but he hadn’t written a word in months. The words had dried up the night his older brother Ravi died—a car accident that shouldn’t have happened, that couldn’t have happened, because Ravi was a careful driver, because the world was supposed to make sense. Arjun had been at his desk, editing a short story, when the phone rang. He remembered the exact sentence he’d been working on, something about a character walking through a park in autumn, and how that sentence now felt like a cruel joke. That was four months ago. Since then, he had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, not just sometimes but always, and that happiness—the kind he used to take for granted—was gone for good.

The shattered beliefs weren’t abstract. They showed up every time he tried to fall asleep. He would lie in bed, unable to relax even knowing the door was locked and his apartment was safe, because safety no longer felt real. Ordinary sounds—a car door outside, a neighbor’s footsteps—made him jump, his heart hammering before his mind could catch up. He knew it was irrational to fear a closing car door, but his body didn’t care. What was rational, anyway, when a loved one could vanish without warning? That line of thinking had become automatic: the world is dangerous, so I cannot relax. It also drove him to ask his friends to reassure him that he was okay, that he wasn’t falling apart, even though he knew he was. He kept cycling through the same question: “Do I seem okay to you?” And they would say yes, but he never believed them, because he could feel the misery pressing down like a weight.

Arjun had stopped making plans for the future. A writing deadline came up and he pushed it back, telling himself he just needed a few days. Then he pushed it back again. He avoided anything that reminded him of Ravi—the coffee shop they used to go to, the playlist they had built together, even certain words that carried his brother’s voice. This avoidance, he believed, was the only way to keep from collapsing entirely. But each time he turned down a friend’s invitation or skipped a meeting, the world felt more dangerous and he felt more broken, as if his own cowardice proved that he could no longer handle life. The more he avoided, the more convinced he became that he had lost himself.

The avoidance also fed his hypervigilance. Because he spent so much time alone in his apartment, trying to control his environment, the smallest unexpected noise became a catastrophe. He would startle, and the startle itself would confirm that he was unsafe, that relaxation was a luxury he could not afford. He tried to rationalize it—it was just the radiator, it was just a car backfiring—but the feeling of danger never abated, and his sleep grew worse. He lay awake night after night, replaying the phone call, watching the words of his story dissolve, wondering if he would ever feel normal again.

What finally brought Arjun to a therapist was the recognition that he had stopped writing, which was the only thing that had ever made him feel like himself. He was terrified that if he returned to the page, he would find nothing there—no sentences, no stories, just the echo of Ravi’s absence. But he was equally terrified of staying stuck. He wanted to believe that recovery was possible, but his shattered beliefs made even that hope feel naive. He sat in the waiting room with his hands on his knees, thinking about the paragraph he had abandoned, and wondered if he could ever finish it.
